text: Lieve Verschuier painted ships, and one of his pictures shows the arrival of Charles II, King of England. He was born in Rotterdam and is recorded in Amsterdam in 1651, where he may have learned to paint from Simon de Vlieger. Two years later he travelled to Rome with Jan Vermeer van Utrecht. Friends there included Willem Drost. He settled in Rotterdam in 1667 and stayed, painting sea scenes and landscapes in the Italian manner. People value his work today for what it shows about building ships in the 17th century.

Margaret Sarah Carpenter painted portraits in the manner of Sir Thomas Lawrence, and she was a close friend of Richard Parkes Bonington. She was born in Salisbury and learned drawing from a local master. Her first studies were copies of the pictures at Longford Castle. The Society of Arts gave her a medal in 1812 and a gold medal two years later. She moved to London in 1814. After that she showed her work at the Royal Academy regularly for almost fifty years.

Ni Zan grew up in a wealthy family in Wuxi, and the money paid for a strict Confucian education. He was born in 1301, soon after Kublai Khan died. The Yuan rulers did not trust many Confucian scholars, so good government jobs were hard to get, and Ni Zan joined a group of wealthy scholars and poets instead. His courtesy name was Yuan Zhen. Together with Huang Gongwang, Wu Zhen and Wang Meng he counts as one of the Four Masters of the Yuan dynasty.

Nicolaes Lauwers engraved prints after paintings by Rubens, Jacob Jordaens and other Flemish masters of his day. He was born in Antwerp and joined the Guild of Saint Luke there in 1619. Soon afterwards he opened a print workshop called In the Writing Hand. In 1635 the guild elected him a deacon. His son Coenraed became an engraver too. Pupils of his included Nicolaes Pitau and Hendrick Snyers.

At thirteen, Philipp Friedrich von Hetsch applied to the Karlsschule in Stuttgart without telling his parents, and the school soon accepted him as a student. His father was a musician at the court of Württemberg. He began with landscapes, but he became known mainly for portraits. His love of the theatre led to a friendship with Friedrich Schiller. At 22 he went to Paris to study under Joseph Marie Vien and Claude Joseph Vernet, and the duke made him court painter later that year. He came home after two years.

Algernon Talmage painted with his left hand because a gun accident in childhood had permanently hurt his right one. The injury also kept him out of active service in the First World War. He studied under Hubert von Herkomer at the Herkomer School in Bushey, next to Lucy Kemp-Welch. From there he moved to St Ives in Cornwall and joined the St Ives School. He founded an artists' club there. Emily Carr was among the students he taught.

Mina Arndt came from a Jewish family near Queenstown in New Zealand, and her father died shortly before she was born. Her mother moved the family to Dunedin, and later Mina took art classes in Wellington. In 1906 she was studying in London under Frank Brangwyn. There she met the printmaker Hermann Struck, who invited her to Berlin to learn etching, which was an honour because he rarely took pupils. She later studied with Lovis Corinth at his art school. Newlyn in Cornwall was another stop, where she worked with Stanhope Forbes.

William Henry Fox Talbot invented the salted paper and calotype processes, two early ways of making photographs. He was a polymath. The Royal Society elected him in 1831 for his work on the integral calculus, and he also researched optics and chemistry. In the 1840s he published The Pencil of Nature, a book illustrated with real prints made from his own negatives. He made early photographs of Oxford, Paris, Reading and York. A patent he held was controversial and affected the first years of commercial photography in Britain.

Abraham van Calraet lived in Dordrecht all his life. He learned to sculpt from AEmilius and Samuel Hup, who were well known sculptors, and then he took up the brush and began by painting fruit while helping his father, a wood sculptor. He may have been a pupil of Aelbert Cuyp, who had the same initials. Cuyp's signature was often forged on top of Calraet's paintings. Abraham Bredius re-attributed two of his still lifes, which people had thought were by Cuyp. A quarrel followed in the Dutch newspapers.

Adolph Friedrich Vollmer was determined to become a painter, even though his father, a bookkeeper to a Hamburg merchant, wanted something else. He grew up in humble circumstances. As a young man he apprenticed with the Suhr brothers, who ran a workshop making panorama prints. He travelled through Germany with Cornelius Suhr for a year and a half. Probably on the advice of the patron Carl Friedrich von Rumohr, he finished his studies in Copenhagen under Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg. Later he moved to Munich and painted landscapes and sea pictures.

Belmiro de Almeida painted, drew, sculpted and made caricatures. His first lessons were at an arts and crafts school in Rio de Janeiro, and after that he studied at the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts. In the late 1880s he travelled to Rome and Paris, where he studied at the Académie Julian and showed his work at several Salons. He fell in love with Paris. From then on he lived in both Paris and Rio de Janeiro, and in 1916 he was appointed to the Chair for drawing from live models.

Carl Hårleman grew up in Stockholm, where his father was head of the royal parks and gardens. He began his architectural training under Göran Josua Adelcrantz. A state scholarship took him abroad in 1721, and he spent four years in Paris at the French academies of architecture and art. Sweden called him home. He was still in Venice in 1727 when the message came. After Nicodemus Tessin the Younger died he became court intendant, and he completed the Royal Palace in Stockholm, which Tessin had begun.

Charlotte Bonaparte sketched Passaic Falls and other American views while she lived in New Jersey with her father. He was Joseph Bonaparte, an older brother of Napoleon, and he had moved to America after the emperor fell. Charlotte stayed with her mother in Europe at first, in Frankfurt, Brussels and Florence. She studied engraving and lithography in Paris. Louis Léopold Robert taught her. She married her first cousin Napoléon Louis in 1826.

Édouard Joseph Dantan came from a family of sculptors, since his grandfather, his father and his uncle all worked in sculpture. He studied in Paris under Isidore Pils and Henri Lehmann. At nineteen he won a commission for a large mural of The Holy Trinity at the Hospice Brezin. His first picture at the Paris Salon showed the destruction of Pompeii. Then the Franco-Prussian War interrupted his work, and he enlisted and rose to lieutenant. His family home burned down.

Edward Radclyffe worked as an engraver, as his father William did before him. He was born in Birmingham in 1809 and trained under his father and Vincent Barber. At fifteen and again at seventeen he won medals from the Society of Arts in London. He moved to London at twenty one. He engraved for the popular annuals and for The Art Journal, and for many years the admiralty paid him to engrave charts. A close friend of David Cox, he also published etchings and engravings of Cox's work.

In 1895 Émile van Ermengem isolated Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium behind botulism, from a piece of ham that had poisoned 34 people. He was born in Leuven and studied in Berlin. Later he became a professor at the University of Ghent. The Académie royale de médecine de Belgique made him a corresponding member in 1887 and a full member in 1902. He died in Ghent. His sons were the writer Franz Hellens and the art critic François Maret.

Evert Breman left Zwolle in 1881 with his younger brother Jacobus, who was known as Co. Co went to Brussels to pursue art. Evert went to Amsterdam, where he apparently worked as a butcher and studied architecture in the evenings. His father's carpentry and blacksmith shop had already taught him some basic building skills. He designed his first buildings in 1886, two homes. Two years later came his first major project, an office building for an insurance company.

Giuseppe Vittore Ghislandi came to be called Fra Galgario, and he worked mainly as a portrait painter in Bergamo. His father was a specialist in quadratura painting, and his brother Defendente was a painter too. He studied first with Giacomo Cotta and then with Bartolomeo Bianchi. In Venice he became a friar of the Order of Minims, yet he kept working as an artist. He spent time in the studio of Sebastiano Bombelli. No early works survive.

Frederick Hollyer photographed paintings and drawings, and he was best known for his copies of Pre-Raphaelite works. He came from a family of engravers, since his father Samuel was a line engraver and three of his brothers worked as engravers too. His first published works were mezzotint engravings after two paintings by Edwin Landseer, in 1869. Photography caught his interest about 1860. Frederic Leighton became his patron. He preferred the platinum print process, which people admired for lasting well.

The son of a goldsmith from Zagreb, Franz Skarbina grew up in Berlin and studied at the Prussian Academy of Arts for four years. After that he spent two years as a tutor to the daughters of a count and travelled to Dresden and Vienna. A study trip through the Netherlands, Belgium and France in 1877 brought him under the influence of impressionism. He went back to Paris and showed at the Salon. In 1888 the Academy made him a professor.

Henry Somm made many etchings for the magazine Paris à l'eau-forte, and he also drew for papers such as Le Chat noir, La Charge and Le Rire. He was born in Rouen, studied at the city's drawing school under Gustave Morin, and moved to Paris in the 1860s. In 1879 Degas invited him to take part in the fourth Impressionist exhibition. He left many drawings and watercolours of Parisian women caught from life. At the Chat noir cabaret he set up a puppet theatre, the first theatre attempt there. Somm never married.

Henryk Szczygliński grew up in Łódź, went to a local drawing school and in 1898 began to study painting in Munich under Stanisław Grocholski. More study followed in Paris and Kraków, where Jacek Malczewski, Leon Wyczółkowski and Jan Stanisławski taught him. He worked with the cabaret Zielony Balonik. In the First World War he served in the Polish Legions, and later he fought against the Bolsheviks. He became president of the Warsaw Artistic Society, and in 1932 the Zachęta gallery gave him an honorary diploma. He died of cancer in 1944.

Georg Wilhelm Issel never had to earn his living by painting, because the court at Darmstadt paid him a fixed salary from 1810. He was the son of a cloth maker, and a family chronicle says his real father was Prince Ludwig himself. He first studied law. In Höchst and Frankfurt he then taught himself drawing and painting. In 1811 he took the young Carl Philipp Fohr into his home in Darmstadt. He travelled to Tyrol with the animal painter Max Josef Wagenbauer, and later trips took him to Paris and Switzerland.

Bengt Nordenberg grew up in poverty in Blekinge as one of nine children and became an apprentice to a painter in Sölvesborg. In 1843 he got his wish to study at the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts in Stockholm. In the autumn of 1851 he went to the Düsseldorf Academy, where Theodor Hildebrandt and later Adolph Tidemand taught him. Tidemand shaped his style, and for a time Nordenberg worked as his assistant and made reproductions of his paintings. He belonged to the Düsseldorf school. His best known pictures are genre scenes of everyday life in Dalarna, Skåne and Blekinge.

Carleton Watkins photographed Yosemite Valley again and again, and his pictures helped to persuade the United States Congress to protect it as a national park. He was born in Oneonta, New York, the eldest of eight children. His father was a carpenter. In 1851 he moved to San Francisco with his childhood friend Collis Huntington and looked for gold. They did not find it, yet both men became successful. Watkins became known for his photography skills.

François van Knibbergen painted landscapes. According to Houbraken he once took part in a painting contest with Jan van Goyen and Jan Porcellis, and the picture by Porcellis was judged the best of the three. The RKD says he was a pupil of Michiel van den Sande in The Hague. In 1614 he travelled with Van den Sande to Rome, and a year later he was back in Utrecht. He joined the Confrerie Pictura in The Hague in 1629. His daughter Catharina also became a landscape painter.

Franz Xaver Wagenschön began as a carriage painter and made portraits of noblemen. He came from Bohemia and went to Vienna in 1747 to attend the art academy, which made him a member in 1770. Paul Troger was also his teacher. He painted portraits of the children of Maria Theresa, especially Marie Antoinette, and in 1763 he painted the panels of the golden Imperialwagen. In later life he made religious and allegorical works influenced by Italian Baroque art. Monasteries and churches such as Göttweig and Poysdorf also ordered pictures from him.

James Heath enjoyed the patronage of George III and of the monarchs after him. He was a bookbinder's son, born in Newgate in London. He was articled to the engraver Joseph Collyer the younger, a strict master who demanded steady work, and Heath gained great mechanical skill in his art. His earliest engravings were portraits in the collected works of Horace Walpole. Next came small illustrations after designs by Thomas Stothard for Bell's Poets of Great Britain and other books, and their taste and dexterity made that kind of illustration popular. He also engraved after Smirke and others.

Jean Bernard Restout nearly lost his life in the Reign of Terror, all because of a favour from Roland. He was born and died in Paris. He won the Prix de Rome in 1758, and after he came back from Italy the Académie royale took him in, but his refusal to follow its rules led to a quarrel. In the Revolution he led the Commune des Arts, which campaigned with David to end the Académie. Roland made him guardian of the royal Garde-Meuble, where a theft later put him under suspicion. He was jailed until the coup of 9 Thermidor.

Jules-Alexandre Grün is best known for a painting called The Dinner Party, made in 1911. He also made posters and illustrations. A large printing company in Paris employed him, and his artistic director there was Jules Chéret. Chéret was also his main competitor in poster art. Some of Grün's posters were published in the series Les Maîtres de l'Affiche, and he is described as a French Post Impressionist painter.

Luigi Garzi moved to Rome at fifteen and became one of the main pupils of Andrea Sacchi. He was born in Pistoia and first learned from a little known landscape painter, Salomon Boccali. He joined Rome's guild of painters, the Accademia di San Luca, in 1670, and the papal society of painters, the Congregazione dei Virtuosi al Pantheon, appointed him its Regent ten years later. Later he worked on the vault frescoes of San Carlo al Corso. Guido Reni strongly influenced his style. He also painted the Glory of the Eternal Father for the dome of the Cybo Chapel.

Marten van Valckenborch painted mainly landscapes and city views. He was born in Leuven into a large Flemish family of artists. Fourteen artists in three generations are recorded in that family. His younger brother Lucas the Elder and his sons Frederik and Gillis were the most important of them. He joined the Guild of Saint Luke in Mechelen in 1559, and in 1563 Gysbrecht Jaspers was recorded as his pupil. Later he moved to Frankfurt.

Neroccio di Bartolomeo de' Landi painted and sculpted in Siena. He studied with Vecchietta and then shared a studio with Francesco di Giorgio. Together they probably made the Scenes from the life of Saint Benedict, now in the Uffizi. In 1472 he painted an Assumption for the abbey of Monte Oliveto Maggiore, and three years later he made a statue of Saint Catherine of Siena for the church in the city that bears her name. They parted ways that year. He later designed the Hellespontine Sybil for the mosaic floor of Siena Cathedral.

Joost van den Vondel wrote a poem about Nicolaes de Helt Stockade, according to Houbraken. Stockade served as court painter to King Louis XIII between 1637 and 1645, and according to the RKD he became a master in the Antwerp Guild of Saint Luke in 1646. He worked on the city hall of Nijmegen and on Amsterdam City Hall. He was a Dutch Golden Age painter.

Otto Eerelman became best known for his pictures of dogs and horses. His father was sexton at the Der Aa church in Groningen, and the boy showed an early talent for art. In 1860 he enrolled at the Academie Minerva against his parents' wishes. He spent another year at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp and later took private lessons in the studio of Lawrence Alma Tadema. In 1867 he began teaching at the Academie in Groningen. He later lived in The Hague, where he became a court painter and portrayed Wilhelmina several times.

Walt Kuhn helped to organize the Armory Show of 1913, which gave America its first large introduction to European Modernism. He grew up near the docks of Red Hook in Brooklyn in a working class family, and nothing in his background suggested a career in art. His first jobs were running a bicycle repair shop and racing bikes. At fifteen he sold his first drawings to a magazine. In 1899 he set out for California with sixty dollars and, once in San Francisco, became an illustrator for WASP Magazine.

As a child, August Piepenhagen was sent to learn the trade of a button and braid maker. He came from a humble family. Later he travelled across Europe, and Switzerland impressed him most, which led him to try painting. He took basic lessons from Johann Heinrich Wüest in Zurich but was otherwise self taught. In 1811 he was in Prague, where a button maker hired him, and when the man died he married the widow and took over the business. He painted more and more, and soon he earned more from his pictures than from his trade.

Claude-Louis Châtelet painted Swiss views and pastoral scenes in the style of Vernet. He was born in Paris in 1753. Examples of his work hang in the Orléans Museum and at the Palace of Fontainebleau. He embraced the Revolution with ardour, allied himself with Robespierre and the Jacobin leaders, and became a member of the Revolutionary Tribunal. Some months after 9 Thermidor he was arrested and condemned. He was executed in Paris in 1795.

Francisco Herrera the Younger fled from Seville to Rome because his father's violent temper had become too much for him. His father, Francisco Herrera the Elder, had taught him first. For six years in Rome he studied architecture, perspective and the antique, since he wanted to paint frescoes. He also painted fish so cleverly that the Romans called him the Spaniard of the Fish. In 1656 he returned to Seville and founded the Seville Academy, and four years later he became its sub director under Murillo. He is said to have been vain.

Juan van der Hamen is remembered mostly for his still lifes, which are also called bodegones. He made the genre popular in Madrid. He was baptised there in 1596 and was probably born just days before. His father was a Flemish courtier who had come from Brussels to serve in the king's noble guard. His mother was half Flemish and came from a noble family of Toledo. He also painted allegories and large works for churches and convents, and his two brothers, Pedro and Lorenzo, were writers.

After his father died, the widowed mother of Justus van Egmont took the family from Leiden back to her native Antwerp when he was 14. His father had been a carpenter. In Antwerp he trained with Gaspar van den Hoecke and worked with Anthony van Dyck, and he also worked in the workshop of Peter Paul Rubens. He moved to France in 1628 and became a court painter for the House of Orléans. There he helped to found the Académie de peinture et de sculpture. Later he came back to Flanders. He is mainly known for portraits.

Fritz Erler designed vases, glass windows and book covers, and later furniture and theatre sets. His first designs date from 1893. He studied under Albrecht Bräuer at the academy in Breslau and also attended the Académie Julian in Paris. In 1895 he moved to Munich, and a year later he was a founding member of the magazine Jugend. Around the start of the century he painted portraits of Richard Strauss and Gerhart Hauptmann. During the First World War he and Arthur Kampf were official military painters, and Erler made war propaganda posters.

Frédéric-Auguste Cazals drew more than 150 portraits of the poet Paul Verlaine, often quick sketches made from life, and he was one of Verlaine's closest friends from 1886 until the poet died. He was born in Paris, taught himself art, and worked for the post office until 1912 to earn his living. He founded the review Le Paris littéraire, which took in Verlaine, Gustave Kahn and Paul Adam. In 1894 he made a poster for the Salon des Cent that shows Verlaine in front and Jean Moréas behind. He also wrote poems.

Gilles-Paul Cauvet was meant for a career in law, but he chose the fine arts instead. He went to Paris while young and became a sculptor, named by the king's brother. He broke with the rococo style. He was born in Aix-en-Provence, and he took part in the decoration of the Palais-Royal and designed furniture, mostly in the Louis XVI style. In 1777 he wrote, drew and published a Recueil d'Ornemens, a book of 64 plates for young artists who wanted to decorate buildings.

Trained by his father Romain, another engraver, Alexis-François Girard worked in the family workshop. They made a series of large head studies after well known paintings of their day, signed Girard et Girard fils. Father and son lived near the Palais de Justice, at one end of the Pont au Change. He was admitted to the Beaux-Arts in Paris in the class of Jean-Baptiste Regnault, but he gave up painting. He married Louise Marthelot in 1820. His son Jules became a Hellenist and a member of the Institut de France.

Henryk Weyssenhoff grew up in the Urals because his father was exiled to Siberia in 1863 for taking part in the January Uprising. His mother followed with the family as far as she could. A fellow exile, Lucjan Kraszewski, gave him his first art lessons. After his father was pardoned the family settled in Warsaw, where he studied with Wojciech Gerson. Henryk Siemiradzki then helped him get into the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg, and he graduated in 1885 with a silver medal. He was an avid hunter. Many of his landscapes show animals.

John Gendall began as a servant, but a man who worked for the print seller Rudolph Ackermann spotted his drawings in a shop. Ackermann brought him to London, where he first filed artists' images and later became a manager and took part in the firm's early experiments with lithography. In 1824 he married the widow of the artist Daniel Havell and went back to Exeter. He was born and died there. He joined W. Cole, who ran the shop where he had been discovered, and later he started an art school.

Joseph Hecht, born in Łódź, taught burin engraving, the classic copper engraving technique, to many artists in his Paris studio, among them Stanley William Hayter. He studied at the art academy in Kraków and then visited museums across Europe. The First World War found him in Berlin, and he spent the war years in neutral Norway. He published his first suite of six prints, l'Arche de Noë, in 1926. Gustave Kahn wrote its preface. In 1927 he encouraged Hayter, and that led to Atelier 17, a cooperative printmaking studio.

Jules Worms came from a family of Parisian shopkeepers and entered the École des Beaux-Arts at seventeen. He made his debut at the Paris Salon ten years later. He is best known for genre scenes of Spanish life, often comical and painted with many details. In the early 1860s he made his first trip to Spain, where he was enchanted by the culture and customs, and he went back six more times to collect sketches and costumes. In 1871 he spent six months in Granada with the Catalan painter Marià Fortuny.

Jojirō Kajita, later known as Kajita Hanko, was the son of a metal engraver in Shitaya in Tokyo. He studied under Ohara Koson. He helped to form several arts organizations and was best known for his illustrations for magazines and newspapers. He married the writer Kitada Usurai in 1898, and they had a child, Hiroe, the next year. Kitada died of intestinal tuberculosis soon afterward. His students included Kokei Kobayashi, Seison Maeda and Togyū Okumura.

Benedetto Caliari came from a family of artists, and his brother was the painter Paolo Veronese. Their father, Gabriele Caliari, was an architect and stonecutter. Benedetto worked with Veronese's sons Carlo and Gabriele, and the three of them were the main helpers in the master's workshop. After Veronese died in 1588 they finished the paintings he had left unfinished. Museums in Bergamo, Cleveland, Saint Petersburg, Vienna and Caen hold works by Benedetto. One of them is in Venice.

Salomon Mesdach lived and worked in Middelburg, and he is known for his portraits. He was active there from 1617 to 1632. Some of his portraits were later engraved. About fifteen of his works are known today. Eight of them hang in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, and one is a family portrait of Guillaume Sweerts in the Haags Historisch Museum. Others belong to the Städel Museum, to a maritime museum in Zeeland and to the museum of fine arts in Valenciennes.

Ivan Khrutsky, also called Jan Chrucki, grew up in a Greek Catholic family in a village in the Vitebsk region, and his father was a priest. He studied privately with George Dawe and then entered the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg. His first known works are dated 1832. Old Woman Knitting a Sock won him the Minor Gold medal of the academy, and in 1839 he received the title of Academician. After his father died he left the city for good and settled on the family estate near Polotsk, where he painted mostly religious art. He died there in 1885.

Fleury-Richard and his friend Pierre Révoil were precursors of the Troubadour style, which had grown out of David's studio. He was the son of a magistrate in Lyon and met Révoil at the drawing school of Alexis Grognard. In 1796 he joined the Paris studio of Jacques-Louis David. Empress Joséphine became his favourite patron. She bought many of his paintings. In 1808 the city of Lyon gave him a studio at the Palais Saint-Pierre because his reputation had brought it benefits, and later he taught at the school of fine arts there.
